The incubation period for the Antipodes parakeet (Cyanoramphus unicolor) has been estimated from data on its congener, the red-crowned parakeet (Cyanoramphus novaezelandiae). Studies indicate that embryonic development within the fertilised ovum requires approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], a condition that promotes optimal organogenesis in the albumen-buffered embryo. Upon hatching, the newly emerged chick first begins to receive parental provisioning, and the initial wet body mass recorded at this stage of first exogenous feeding is remarkably modest. The hatchling weighs only 7.68 grams [Ww0 = 7.68 grams], a value that underscores the altricial state of the nestling and the considerable energetic investment required from both parents during the subsequent brooding and feeding periods. This low birth mass is comparable to values reported for other members of the genus, which typically produce small, rapidly growing chicks that depend heavily on crop milk and regurgitated food during their early development within the nest cavity.

Sexual dimorphism in body size becomes apparent as the nestling chick matures into a fully grown adult. Field surveys and captive colony measurements have established that the ultimate wet body mass, representing the asymptotic adult size, differs markedly between the sexes. Adult females attain a maximum body mass of approximately 133 grams [Wwi = approximately 133 grams], a figure that reflects the typical energetic constraints and reproductive demands placed on the breeding female. In contrast, reproductively active adult males are consistently heavier, reaching an ultimate body mass of around 167 grams [Wwi = around 167 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males being roughly 25 percent heavier than females, is a notable feature of the species and may be linked to male-male competition for access to nesting territories and mates during the breeding season. The dimorphism is similar in magnitude to that observed in other large-bodied Cyanoramphus species occupying subantarctic islands.

Under the thermoneutral conditions characteristic of this species' active metabolic range, typically measured at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], several key life-history transitions have been documented. The fledgling, having achieved full flight feather maturation, departs the nest at 52.5 days after hatching [tx = 52.5 days after hatching], a duration that aligns with the extended nestling periods seen in other subantarctic parrots and likely reflects the slow growth rates imposed by the cool, resource-poor island environment at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Sexual maturation, marked by the onset of gonadal swelling and the initial development of reproductive tissues, occurs considerably later. Puberty is reached at approximately 157 days after hatching [tp = approximately 157 days after hatching], a timing that allows the juvenile bird to complete its somatic growth and accumulate sufficient body reserves through the post-fledging dispersal and winter foraging periods before the energetic demands of repr at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]oduction begin.

The Antipodes parakeet is an exceptionally long-lived bird for its body size, a life-history strategy common among subantarctic avifauna that face unpredictable food resources and harsh climatic conditions. Captive individuals and field-based longevity estimates indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan in this species, measured at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], is an impressive 6,826 days [am = 6,826 days], which is equivalent to roughly 18.7 years. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a delayed onset of breeding. The first successful nesting event, representing the time since birth at first brood, does not occur until the bird is approximately 584 days after hatching [tR = approximately 584 days after hatching], a value that reflects the slow pace of life i at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]n this species. The combination of delayed maturity, low annual fecundity, and remarkable longevity is a classic example of a slow life-history strategy, likely an evolutionary response to the stable but low-productivity environment of the Antipodes Islands.

Reproductive output in the Antipodes parakeet is constrained by both the limited clutch size and the infrequency of nesting attempts in the cool subantarctic climate. Females typically lay a clutch of three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three eggs per clutch] each breeding season, a modest number compared to temperate-zone parrots. Furthermore, the species produces only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], resulting in a very low annual reproductive rate that is consistent with the slow life-history pace described earlier. Basal metabolic rate, measured as oxygen consumption in resting adults under thermoneutral conditions at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], has been recorded at 194.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 194.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This rate is relatively low for a parrot of this body mass and may represent an adaptive metabolic depression that reduces daily energetic costs of tissue upkeep during the long, cold winters when food availability is scarce. The combination of low fecundity, high adult survival, and a reduced metabolic rate is a common energetic syndrome among island-endemic birds that face limited and unpredictable food supplies.
